newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: PRESS DIGEST - Czech Republic - Jan 3.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Czech Republic - Jan 3.

text.p: MLADA FRONTA DNES - The Czech Finance Ministry claimed a 419 million surplus in the 1996 state budget because it sold three billion crowns in treasury bills to cover an expected deficit.

HOSPODARSKE NOVINY - The supply of Russian crude will not mirror the situation in January 1996, when supplies stopped for 10 days due to Ukrainian dmeands for higher transit tariffs, according to Ales Soukup, a spokesman for Ceska Rafinerska a.s..

- The Czech Association of Industry and Transportation has opened an office in Brussels, according to the director of the office, Petr Pomezny. The opening is one of the steps planned to support Czech exports.
- Preliminary results indicate that engineering conglomerate CKD Holding should have a gross profit of 600 to 700 million crowns and a net profit of approximately 200 million crowns.

- Representatives of large banks are more or less reserved when rating 1996's economic results. Monetary institutions faced restrictive measures from the Czech National Bank and unfavourable conditions on the capital market.

Ceska Sporitelna general director Jaroslav Klapal said that 1996 gross profit would be roughly one billion crowns higher than the originally forecast 5.9 billion crowns, but said reserves to cover interbank trading would be higher than expected. He did not give a net profit forecast.
- Nissan has lowered the price of their automobiles on the Czech market by 10,000 to 30,000 crowns, according to the company's assistant economic manager, Zdenek Fort.
Mitsubishi also decided to lower their prices, though the import manager of Honda's Czech operations stated that this does not indicate a price war but simply reflects the lower value of the Yen.

- According to a poll, people are more pessimistic about the new year than they were a year ago. At the beginning of 1996 56 percent of the people polled expected the coming year would be good while only 47 percent of those polled this year expected 1997 to be good.
- Vladimir Stehlik offered to step down from the purchase contract for Poldi Ocel, according to Stehlik's lawyer, Jiri Teryngel.

Stehlik, in a letter to Holding Kladno, the National Property Fund and the Ministry of Trade and Industry, has requested one billion and six million crowns plus interest and has also requested to be paid for the know-how he brought to Poldi, according to Martin Hort, the National Property Fund's representative in Poldi. Stehlik does expect to also make up for changes in the company's balance since he took over.
- The new country-wide television station, Prima TV, will begin broadcasting today. It will be replacing Premiera TV which ended its three and a half year history yesterday.

- SPT Telecom will delay its entry to the Internet market, originally planned for January, 1997. The delay should not be longer than one or two months, according to Kevin Caruso, the director of business services.
- K-Petrol a.s., the second largest chain of filling stations, is expecting sales to exceed 2.7 billion crowns, an increase of 70 percent over 1995.

PRAVO - Eurotel has almost fulfilled the condition that 80 percent of the population have access to their GSM network by the end of June, 1997. According to their most recent information, the company is accessible to 75 percent of the population.
- The Czech Republic is 30th of 54 countries in terms of corruption, according to research undertaken by Transparency International, headquartered in Berlin. -- Prague Newsroom, +42-2-2423-0003
